newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Politicians press for delay in Liberian election.
newsitem.headline: Politicians press for delay in Liberian election.

text.p: Twelve of the 13 political parties contesting Liberia's July 19 election are pressing for a postponement of the poll because of alleged irregularities.
Leading presidential contender Charles Taylor opposes a delay.

Many Liberians fear that controversy over the election date could plunge the West African nation, founded in 1847 by freed American slaves, into renewed conflict after a delicately negotiated accord to end seven years of civil war.
Representatives of the parties, except for Taylor's National Patriotic Front of Liberia, called for the postponement at meetings on Friday and Saturday.
They suggested no new date for the poll, intended to wrap up the faltering regional process designed to bring peace to Liberia.
Party spokesmen said a new date would be put forward after another meeting scheduled for Monday.

"There was a general consensus in the meeting that elections be delayed because there are frauds in the process leading up to the elections," said Cletus Wotorson, the presidential candidate of the Alliance Party.

"The conduct of the polls on the 19th may be free and fair, but the process leading to the date is fraudulent," he told reporters, displaying a voter card he said he was given in Abidjan, Ivory Coast, where they were printed.

"We are not going to be a part of a game that is not free and fair and whose winner would say that we participated. We are not going to go to elections on July 19," said presidential candidate Chea Cheapoo of the Progressive People's Party.
Western diplomats whose governments are helping fund the poll have cautioned about donor fatigue, and may still be able to exert some leverage to ensure that the election stays on course.
"I think it would be a tragedy if something went wrong that it was impossible to hold elections on time," said U.S. Ambassador William Milam.

"I need to tell you in fact that all of the governments involved really can't afford now to have the elections postponed by very long, because so much money has been put into it that we won't be able to recover," Milam told Monrovia's Inquirer newspaper.

The peace plan brokered by the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) scheduled the poll and set the swearing in of an elected president for August 2, if a winner emerges with more than 50 percent of the votes.

The elections commission headed by veteran journalist Henry Andrews is reported to have told the parties to decide themselves and forward their request to ECOWAS, which sent a Nigerian-led ECOMOG peacekeeping force to Liberia in 1990.

"The elections committee and the parties are not ready for these elections," said George Boley, an influential leader of the militarily strong Krahn tribe and presidential candidate of the National Democratic Party.

"Up to now there has been no voters' register in the southeast of this country. How can we hold elections when some parties have no access to a large portion of the country?" Boley told reporters after Saturday's meeting.

Taylor, who launched a civil war in December 1989 and is confident of winning the presidential election, is pressing ahead with campaigning. He was not available for comment on the growing pressure from his rivals for a poll delay.
In addition to Taylor and Boley, a third powerful warlord -- Alhaji Kromah of the mainly Moslem Mandigo ULIMO party -- is running for the presidency.

The most serious civilian contender is former United Nations official Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf. She is the only woman in the contest and potentially the toughest rival to Taylor, according to local political commentators.
